where: the header state badge, the consequence strip and the merge picker's heading, on the expiring, duplicate and push-failed cards
finding: The three tiers are meant to say three different kinds of thing — what the state is, what approving costs, what is true of one child — but all three are painted in the same accent at the same intensity, so a card reads as one alarm restated three times rather than a chain. The badge and the strip are effectively the same swatch (same text colour, same ring, a five-percent difference in tint) sitting twelve pixels apart, so the eye takes them as a single amber region at the top of the card and stops reading either as a distinct statement. Tier three then repeats it: the round neutralised the row badges but left the picker's heading in the state colour, so the row's voice is half neutral by policy and half alarm.
evidence: On the expiring card, the warn chip '4 days left' sits directly above a two-line warn panel set in warn text on a warn ring, and a hundred pixels below that 'One student on the roster shares this name.' is warn again — three amber objects, three sizes, one hue. The push-failed card repeats the pattern in red. The sibling-join card is the counter-proof: a neutral strip under a neutral chip reads immediately as state-then-consequence, because only one thing in the pair is trying to be the alarm.
direction: Let the accent own exactly one tier, and let position and container carry the rest. The chip is the natural owner — it is the state, in two or three words. Take the consequence strip down to the neutral panel treatment the sibling-join card already demonstrates, and take the picker heading down to the row's neutral voice, the same move the round already made on the row badges. One coloured object per card is what makes the colour worth looking at.

where: the armed foot — Cancel, the sentence, and the commit
finding: Every other decision on this page is a caption sitting on top of the button it describes; that contract is the whole idea of the round. The armed block breaks it. It opens with Cancel, then the sentence, then the commit — so the one sentence on the page that says the action cannot be taken back is positioned as a caption of the button above it. The block's internal gaps are uniform, so nothing resolves the ambiguity: the sentence is equidistant from the button it belongs to and the button it does not. It also sets that sentence two steps larger than every resting caption and abandons the two-column foot entirely, so the card that most needs to look like the same object in a different mode is the one that looks like a different component.
evidence: On phone the sequence is a full-width Cancel, then the consequence sentence, then a full-width Yes — the retreat arriving first and at the same weight as the commit, reversing the primary-then-secondary order used on all four other cards. The sentence is 14px where every resting caption is 12px, and the tinted, ringed panel it sits in is the same shape used for the consequence strip at the top of the other cards, so the armed foot reads as a strip that slid to the bottom rather than as a state change.
direction: Keep the foot's own grammar when it arms. Nothing should sit above the sentence; the sentence belongs immediately above the commit, at the caption size the resting foot uses. Put the retreat after the commit, or beside it in the slot the resting foot already gives its second instrument, so the armed state reads as the same object changing rather than two components swapping.

where: the end-of-queue note in the trailing grid cell
finding: The note is stretched to the full height of its row, so the largest object on the page — about 560px tall, a third of the scroll — is an empty dashed rectangle with one line of grey text floating in the middle of it. A dashed, card-shaped, card-sized box inside a grid of cards reads as a slot waiting for a card, which is the opposite of what its text says. It is also stranded: the card above it ends 190px higher, so the right column below the fold is roughly 750px of near-nothing with fourteen pixels of text in it.
evidence: Measured, the dashed box runs from y=1311 to y=1874 while the card above it ends at y=1121; the only content inside is the single line 'That is all 5. Nothing else is waiting to be reviewed.', vertically centred in 560px of void.
direction: Stop the note pretending to be a card. Let it size to its own text, lose the dashed border that reads as a placeholder, and let it sit as a quiet full-width line beneath the last row rather than occupying a cell — which also closes the stranded gap the trailing cell creates in the right column.

where: the two-up merge candidates on the duplicate card
finding: Side by side, the two candidates keep the gap they had when stacked on phone, so the pair reads as one wide control with a seam down it rather than as two competing choices — which is precisely the distinction the reader has to make here. In the same card the foot's two columns are 24px apart and the page's gutter is 32px, so the tightest gutter on the screen falls between the two things that most need to be told apart.
evidence: The two candidate buttons' borders are four pixels apart; their labels differ only in the final two words, so there is almost nothing but that hairline separating them.
direction: Give the horizontal pair a gutter from the same family as the foot's columns, so two boxes read as two objects. The vertical gap between stacked options can stay tight — it is only the side-by-side case that needs the air.

where: the merge picker's rule, heading and subline
finding: The picker is meant to be indented to the child's name column and lands twelve pixels short of it — indented by the avatar's width but not by the gap that follows the avatar. The candidate buttons' labels do land on the name column, so the block ends up with three left edges instead of two, and the amber heading is the one poking out to the left of every piece of text it belongs to.
evidence: On the duplicate card the child's name, grade and allergy share one left edge; the rule beneath them and the picker's heading begin 12px to the left of it; then the candidate label inside the button returns to the original edge. The same 12px stagger appears on the expiring card at both viewports.
direction: Indent the picker's rule and its two lines of text to the name column itself, so the picker hangs under the name it is about and the row block has two edges — avatar, then names — rather than three.

where: the three-instrument foot on the push-failed card
finding: The first instrument spans the foot, so its caption is set at roughly twice the measure of the two beneath it — about eighty characters a line against about forty. Within one object the same class of text changes measure mid-read, and the wide line is past the length a caption gets finished. The button under it is auto-width, so the thing that actually spans is the paragraph, not the instrument: the foot reads as a wide paragraph, then a medium button, then a tidy two-column pair — a pile rather than a set.
evidence: The first caption runs the full 528px width of the foot on one line, while the second wraps at half that a few pixels below it.
direction: Hold every caption in the foot to one measure. Either let the primary instrument occupy a single column and run its caption taller rather than wider, or cap the spanning caption at the column measure, so the foot presents one text column width from top to bottom.

where: the neutral header badge against the neutral row badges
finding: The header state badge and the row fact badge are the same object — same shape, radius, size, fill, ring and weight. When a state happens to be neutral, tier one and tier three become distinguishable only by where they sit, which means the form carries none of the tier information the system claims to encode. A reader scanning the column gets no cue for 'this is what the card is' versus 'this is what already happened to one child'.
evidence: 'Joins a family on file' in the sibling-join header and 'Merged' in the expiring card's first row render as identical chips; only their position tells you one describes a family and the other describes a single row.
direction: Separate the two roles by form rather than by placement. Keep the filled, ringed pill for the header state and let the row's fact drop to a plain quiet label without a container — the row already owns its own control and does not need to borrow the header's shape to be read.
